The programme is expected to have Mr. Rajmohan, Minister for Art and Culture, as the Chief Guest. It will begin with a lament reflecting on the present state of the arts, followed by an inquiry into the lament and the larger condition of artistic traditions. This will be followed by a special address by the Chief Guest.

The programme will also include the release of publications developed through the work of the collaborating organisations. Among them is a bilingual field manual for documenting and digitising performing arts, developed from the Suvadugal team’s field experience and internal documentation and now being published as a practical toolkit. A publication emerging from the team’s contribution to the development of curriculum for art education will also be released.

Alongside the formal sessions, the event will feature a flash folk performance, an exhibition featuring work from collaborating organisations, and a live 3D-scanning demonstration by the Suvadugal team, presenting some of the documentation and digitisation practices being developed through the initiative.

The programme will conclude with a panel discussion on Art and Policy, bringing together questions of artistic practice, documentation, education, cultural preservation, and the role of public policy in supporting the arts.

content.markdown:
The Department of Humanities & Social Sciences, IIT Kharagpur is pleased to issue a Call for Papers  for an **NPTEL-ICSSR-sponsored Three-Day National Conference and Workshop** titled **“Voices & Traditions: Knowing Andamans through Language & Culture”** to be held from the **3rd to the 5th November, 2026**. There will also be a preconference workshop and hands-on training in **[LiFE Suite](https://life.unreal-tece.co.in)** for data elicitation and annotation. 

The conference wants to bring scholars of linguistics, anthropology, sociology and scholars from other disciplines who are working with the speech communities of Andaman and Nicobar Islands to share their experiences and insights about their research. There will be panel discussions and oral paper presentations. The keynote speaker for the conference is Padma Shree Prof Anvita Abbi. There will be other eminent speakers as well who will be talking about data elicitation, ethical practices of the field and data analysis.

Aiming to bridge interdisciplinary research on the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, this conference provides a collaborative forum for scholars documenting indigenous languages, oral narratives, and cultural heritage. Through paper presentations and panel discussions, participants will share vital insights on language and culture shift, data elicitation, ethical protocols, heritage preservation, and community-engaged research across the islands.

We invite original, unpublished research papers on topics including, but not limited to:


- Language Documentation & Description: Grammatical analysis, phonology, lexicography, and cultural practices.


- Oral Literature & Folklore


- Sociolinguistics & Language Shift: Language vitality, Music vitality, and other related areas.


- Fieldwork Ethics & Methodologies: Ethical protocols, community involvement, data management, and digital archiving.


- Ethnocultural, Anthropological & Sociological Studies: Interdisciplinary perspectives on social structures, indigenous knowledge systems, and cultural practices.


The topic of the paper should** focus on communities of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands**.

Please submit an anonymous abstract of 300 words as a PDF document to the following email by the given deadline - [andamanlanguageandculture@gmail.com](mailto:andamanlanguageandculture@gmail.com)

Kindly provide author details and institutional affiliation **only **in the body of the email, **not in the abstract itself**.

You can send one single-authored and/or one joint authored abstract.

All the participants who are attending in person will need to register for the conference and the workshop.

content.markdown:
Arunachal Pradesh and the wider Eastern Himalayan and Northeast Indian region constitute one of the world’s most linguistically and culturally diverse landscapes. The region is home to numerous tribal communities, oral traditions, indigenous languages and endangered varieties. Much of this intangible cultural heritage, including oral narratives, ritual language, folk music and community knowledge, remains undocumented or is preserved only in fragile, non-digital formats, making it vulnerable to loss across generations.

At the same time, developments in digital documentation, data management and artificial intelligence are creating new possibilities for the systematic documentation, organization, archiving and revitalization of endangered languages and cultural resources.
In this context, RIWATCH, Roing and CoDIN is jointly organizing a two-day workshop-cum-training programme for researchers, scholars, students and community stakeholders. The programme will introduce participants to practical methods of digital documentation and archiving, including principles of visual documentation, metadata creation, structured transcription, data organization and the use of SayMore. It will also provide an introductory, hands-on orientation to AI-assisted language documentation suite the LIFE platform, including Atekho and Matra Lab.

The workshop is designed to be practical and participatory. Participants will work with their own pre-recorded language and cultural materials, reflect on their documentation practices, and develop basic, structured digital documentation packages. The programme will also address ethical, legal and community-consent considerations in the use and archiving of indigenous language and cultural data.

content.teaser: Data Sovereignty, Data Quality and Indigenous Communities
content.markdown:
## The Goal

In today's AI-driven world, the digital divide is rapidly evolving into a profound social and economic divide. Despite our diverse real world, the digital landscape remains largely monolithic and non-inclusive. This lack of representation affects communities, languages, and cultures that don't fit the dominant technological paradigm.

Governments, civil society organisations, communities, and individuals are increasingly concerned about how sociocultural norms, languages, practices, and identities are represented in AI systems.
There's a pressing need for sensitive, unbiased representation that reflects our world's true diversity, not just the perspectives of dominant group.


## The Cost 

Despite numerous initiatives to create more inclusive AI systems, these efforts often fall short due to insufficient quality training data that properly represents diverse languages and cultures. Documentation shows that up to 35-40% of originally collected data must be discarded due to quality issues, even with robust methodologies and reputable organizations involved. This entails a huge cost in terms of time and resources involved in creating datasets. As a result, only few languages and communities could be supported in the technological world.


## The Gap

Currently, speech and language data collection is primarily handled by organisations, individuals and community members with little to no experience or training required for working with indigenous, underserved communities, resulting in fundamental misunderstandings of its unique requirements.

- **General annotation firms** lack specific training in working with diverse, indigenous communities.
- While skilled in community engagement, **civil society and community-based professionals** typically lack an understanding of linguistic complexity and linguistic field research expertise.
- **Language Promotion Organizations** are often focused on promoting specific language varieties rather than capturing linguistic diversity, thereby, filtering out, instead of collecting the required dataset.
- Even **academic departments** frequently lack proper fieldwork training and methodology for this specialized work.


## The W2M Intervention

The W2M Academy has designed this specialised course for training community members, researchers, civil society members and other stakeholders, who are engaged in or are planning to get engaged in data collection or AI model development. The course will train participants in the methods and practice of large-scale linguistic data collection and AI model development with indigenous communities. With our experts who have been working in linguistic field methods, language documentation and language technologies of indigenous and underserved communities for over a decade, this training and certification program aims to fill the community training and data quality gap.

projects.title: Suvadugal
projects.description: A government-supported cultural expression documentation and digital archiving initiative focused on preserving the traditional arts, performances, musical instruments, artist histories, and cultural knowledge systems of Tamil Nadu’s Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe communities. The project contributes to the safeguarding and long-term preservation of intangible cultural heritage in line with broader UNESCO cultural heritage preservation goals.
projects.longDescription:
Suvadugal (meaning ‘traces’ or ‘footprints’) is a large-scale cultural heritage documentation and digital archiving initiative implement through the collaboration with Alternative Media Centre, India’s largest folk artist collective. The project is funded by the Adi Dravidar and Tribal Welfare Department and supported by the Directorate of Tribal Welfare, Government of Tamil Nadu.

The initiative focuses on documenting, preserving, and creating long-term public access to the diverse traditional art forms, performance traditions, musical instruments, oral narratives, artist histories, and cultural spaces associated with Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe communities across Tamil Nadu. Particular emphasis is placed on communities, practices, and knowledge systems that remain vulnerable, under-documented, or at risk of disappearance.

Suvadugal combines ethnographic field documentation, archival preservation methods, multimedia recording, metadata-driven cataloguing, and emerging digital preservation technologies such as photogrammetry and 3D digitization. The project aims to create a sustainable and publicly accessible digital repository that captures not only cultural objects and performances, but also the relationships between artists, spaces, instruments, rituals, and communities.

The project follows a post-custodial approach to cultural archiving, recognizing that cultural knowledge and heritage remain closely tied to the communities and practitioners from whom they emerge. Documentation practices are designed to be collaborative and community-engaged rather than extractive. The Alternative Media Centre collective of artists plays a key role in supporting documentation, interpretation, artist engagement, and collaborative field practices throughout the project.

Rather than functioning as a static archive, Suvadugal is designed as a relational cultural knowledge system that supports research, education, public engagement, and future cultural preservation efforts, while contributing to broader conversations around safeguarding intangible cultural heritage.
projects.methodology:
The project follows a field-based and metadata-centered documentation methodology integrating audiovisual recording, photography, oral history collection, transcription, cataloguing, metadata design, and digital preservation workflows. High-fidelity audio-visual documentation, photogrammetry, and 3D scanning are used to preserve both performances and cultural objects.

The archival platform is structured around interconnected cultural entities such as art forms, performances, artists, instruments, and cultural spaces. The project follows a post-custodial documentation approach in which communities, artists, and practitioners remain central to how cultural knowledge is represented and preserved. Collaborative field documentation practices involving artists, researchers, and community members form a core part of the project methodology.

projects.longDescription:
Tholkudi is a large-scale language and cultural documentation initiative supported by the Government of Tamil Nadu and developed to document, preserve, and improve long-term access to the linguistic and cultural heritage of Scheduled Tribe communities across Tamil Nadu.

The project brings together language documentation, oral traditions, folklore, ecological knowledge, songs, narratives, ritual practices, material culture, and community histories into a structured digital archival environment intended for long-term preservation and public accessibility.

Karthick Narayanan served as consultant for language documentation and played a major role in shaping the archive’s documentation architecture, metadata approach, multilingual archival structure, and broader conceptual direction. His work contributed substantially to the development of the archive’s documentation workflows and approaches to representing linguistic and cultural knowledge within a digital archival system.

In continuation of this work, the Council for Diversity and Innovation (CoDIN) was later entrusted with implementing a user-centered redesign and accessibility-oriented archival interface for the repository. This phase focused on improving discoverability, metadata navigation, browsing systems, multilingual accessibility, mobile responsiveness, and overall public usability of archival collections.

The redesign process emphasized practical archival usability for researchers, students, educators, government stakeholders, and community members while maintaining compatibility with long-term digital preservation standards.

The project combines field documentation, digital humanities approaches, metadata-driven archival systems, and participatory methods of cultural preservation. Particular emphasis is placed on ensuring that archival representation remains context-sensitive, community-informed, and publicly accessible.

Rather than functioning solely as a storage repository, Tholkudi is envisioned as a living cultural knowledge platform supporting research, education, cultural continuity, public engagement, and future heritage preservation initiatives related to Tamil Nadu’s indigenous and tribal communities.

projects.title: Supporting Informed Orthographic Choice for Unwritten Languages
projects.description: A sub-project under the project titled, From Voice to Script: Revitalising Mother Tongues through Indic Orthographic Development in North-East India, funded by the Government of India, to develop transcribed speech data, a phonemic inventory, Latin and Devanagari orthographic representations, comparative reading-evaluation results, and, where required, Unicode keyboard support, user documentation, and a digital Varnmala primer for 5 languages of Arunachal Pradesh
projects.longDescription:
## Rationale and Conceptual Basis

Northeast India is characterised by extensive linguistic diversity, multilingualism and multiscriptality. Across the region, language communities use Roman, Indic and indigenous scripts in different historical, educational, cultural and technological settings. Many communities also remain primarily oral or use writing practices that are not yet stable across domains. In such settings, orthography development cannot be reduced to the technical selection of symbols. It is simultaneously a linguistic, educational, technological and social intervention (Robinson & Gadelii, 2003; Jones & Mooney, 2017; Pandey, 2021).

The project therefore brings together speech documentation, IPA transcription, phonetic and phonological analysis, orthography methodology and candidate development, psycholinguistic/learnability evaluation, comparative evidence, and digital implementation. These components correspond directly to the scientific and technical functions identified in the project framework. The approach is also community-consultative. Community engagement, participation of native speakers and language experts, documented willingness, review and validation form part of the project process.

Accordingly, the project treats orthography development as a connected process moving from speech documentation and linguistic analysis to orthographic representation, evaluation, digital implementation and community review and validation.

## Aim and Objectives

**Aim:** To develop and comparatively evaluate practical orthographic solutions for participating languages of Arunachal Pradesh, and to provide comparative evidence and project outputs for community review and validation.


**Program Objectives**

- Establish a participatory orthography-development process in which community willingness, consultation, review and validation form part of the development process.

- Collect and prepare a documented speech corpus with consent, speaker and context metadata for each participating language.

- Produce reviewed IPA transcription and phonetic and phonological descriptions sufficient to identify orthographically relevant contrasts and requirements.

- Develop candidate orthographic representations from the linguistic analysis and subject them to iterative community review before testing.

- Prepare matched learning materials and conduct comparative evaluation of candidate systems.

- Implement candidate systems digitally through input, font/rendering and Unicode-compatibility work as required for comparative testing and practical use.

- Produce comparative evidence, facilitate community review and validation, refine the orthographic and technical outputs as required, and provide the agreed project data, technical documentation and outputs for handover.


## Deliverables

The project will produce the following deliverables and programme outputs for each of the five languages:

- 50 hrs of transcribed speech data in 5 languages.
- Phonemic Inventory in 5 languages.
- Orthographic Representation in Latin and Devanagari for each language.
- Results of the comparative reading evaluation for Latin and Devanagari orthographic representations in each language.
- Unicode keyboard for the chosen orthographic representation in each language, wherever required.
- User Manual for the Keyboard.
- Reading material – Digital Varnmala Primer in each language.
projects.methodology:
## Community-First Participation Process for Language Selection

Participation begins before the participating languages are finalised. Communities will receive an accessible explanation of the research process, expected time commitments, remuneration, data use, controlled evaluation, and anticipated outputs before any expression of willingness is recorded. Community representatives will be given adequate time to consult internally with their respective communities. Attendance at the workshop will not, by itself, constitute community consent or agreement to participate. Formal willingness to participate will be sought only after the workshop and following the community’s internal consultation process.

Community participation continues throughout the programme. Community language experts contribute linguistic judgements, examples and local usage knowledge; review candidate orthographies; contribute to learning materials; assess clarity and naturalness; and participate in community review and validation.

## Linguistic validity and orthographic representation

Linguistic analysis will be grounded in recorded speech and reviewed IPA transcription. The working target is approximately 50 speakers per language, contributing about one recorded hour each, yielding approximately 50 hours of speech per language, and 250 hours across the five-language programme. Sampling will seek to capture relevant geographical, generational and social variation within each participating language community.
Data collection will combine app-based participation with assisted fieldwork, allowing the programme to accommodate both independently recorded contributions and recordings requiring field-based support. Elicitation will draw on complementary task types, including translation, picture description, visual and wordless-story narration or retelling, monologues, and targeted linguistic elicitation. Recordings will be organised with the relevant speaker, consent, contextual and task metadata and prepared for IPA transcription and review.
The reviewed corpus will provide the empirical basis for phonetic and phonological analysis. Phonetic description will document the phones occurring in the language and relevant patterns of variation. Phonological analysis will identify phonemes, allophonic relationships, distributional patterns, syllable structure, and relevant segmental and suprasegmental contrasts, including tone or stress where applicable. Analysis may proceed alongside continuing transcription and collection, with targeted supplementary elicitation undertaken where the emerging analysis identifies gaps or unresolved contrasts.

Orthographic representation will therefore be developed from the linguistic analysis rather than from a prior preference for a particular script or spelling convention. Candidate mappings will be constructed to represent the linguistically relevant contrasts identified in the language, together with the rules required for their consistent use. Community language experts will subsequently review these candidates for acceptability, usability, correspondence with local language intuitions, and compatibility with existing practices where relevant. Their feedback will inform revision of the candidates before they proceed to comparative learning, usability and digital evaluation.

## Learnability and Controlled Psycholinguistic Evaluation

Candidate orthographies will be evaluated not only for linguistic adequacy and community acceptability, but also for how effectively language users can learn, recognise, read and produce the proposed representations. The precise experimental design will be developed after the linguistic characteristics of each language and the relevant candidate systems have been established. The evaluation will remain writing-system-agnostic, referring to symbols, written forms, and orthographic representations rather than presupposing a particular type of script.

A set of complementary psycholinguistic tasks may be used to examine different dimensions of orthographic processing. Read-aloud tasks will compare reading performance across candidate systems using matched words or passages. Where repeated exposure to the same material may create memory effects, different passages may be used while embedding common control items. Stimuli may be balanced for high- and low-frequency words and phonemes, as well as for syllable complexity and the complexity of the corresponding written representation. Performance will be assessed primarily in terms of reading speed, fluency, and accuracy.

Rapid Automatized Naming (RAN) tasks may be used to examine the speed and automaticity of participants' retrieval of well-learned linguistic information from familiar visual stimuli. Depending on the stage of learning and the nature of the candidate system, these tasks may use grids containing familiar images, written forms or other appropriately learned items.

Image–orthography matching tasks may examine how readily familiar concepts are associated with alternative written representations. Participants may be shown images of commonly known objects, along with corresponding forms in the candidate systems, and asked to select the representation they consider most appropriate or accurate. Stimulus sets may be designed to include phonemes or contrasts that are particularly relevant to the orthographic analysis.

Auditory–orthography matching tasks will examine the relationship between spoken language and proposed written forms. Participants may hear a spoken word or other auditory stimulus and identify the corresponding written representation from alternatives presented in the candidate systems. These tasks can provide comparative evidence on how clearly different orthographic representations correspond to the forms perceived in speech.
Writing and written-form evaluation tasks may examine both orthographic production and subsequent interpretation. Participants may be asked to write spoken words using different candidate systems, with particular attention to low-frequency phonemes or contrasts represented through more complex symbol combinations. The resulting forms may then be read or evaluated by other language users, who may either choose between alternatives or rate the perceived accuracy of the written form. This allows the programme to examine both the production of orthographic forms and their interpretation by other users.

Across these task families, stimulus selection will be controlled, as far as practicable, for factors that may independently influence performance, including word frequency, phoneme frequency, familiarity, syllable complexity and representational complexity. Experimental findings will therefore not be interpreted solely from raw differences in speed, accuracy or preference where those differences may be attributable to characteristics of the linguistic material or to participants’ prior familiarity with particular writing systems.

The different tasks address related but distinct aspects of orthographic usability. Read-aloud and RAN tasks provide evidence of fluency, accuracy, and automaticity; image- and auditory-matching tasks examine the perceived correspondence between linguistic forms and written representations; and writing tasks provide evidence of productive use and interpretability. The results will be considered alongside the linguistic analysis, community review, and digital implementation findings, rather than reduced to a single numerical ranking of candidate systems.

The psycholinguistic evaluation will therefore follow directly from the linguistic analysis: the phonological analysis identifies what must be represented, candidate orthographies provide alternative solutions, and controlled evaluation examines how effectively language users process and use those alternatives.

## Digital Accessibility and Implementation

Digital accessibility will be treated as part of orthographic evaluation rather than as a technical step undertaken only after a writing system has been selected. Candidate orthographies must be reliably displayed, entered, edited, and exchanged in the digital environments where communities are likely to use them, including smartphones, computers, web-based applications, and common communication platforms. Basic digital support, therefore, requires attention not only to character encoding, but also to font coverage, text rendering and practical input mechanisms.

For each candidate orthography, the technical team will first examine the character repertoire and its compatibility with Unicode. Wherever possible, representations will make appropriate use of characters and character sequences already available in Unicode. Character selection will consider not only visual appearance but also the characters' underlying properties and intended behaviour. Candidate forms, particularly those involving diacritics or combining marks, will be tested across relevant fonts, devices and software environments to identify rendering or interoperability problems at an early stage. Unicode guidance specifically recommends such testing during orthography development rather than after an orthography has been finalised.

The programme will develop and test candidate-specific input solutions, including keyboard layouts suitable for desktop and mobile use. Layouts will be designed around the actual character inventory and frequency of use within each orthography, with attention to the efficient entry of diacritics, multicharacter sequences or other representations required by the language. Cross-platform keyboard standards similarly recognise input support as a central component of digital language enablement, rather than an optional addition to character encoding.
Where existing fonts do not adequately support the required characters or combinations, the programme will undertake font adaptation and rendering work and test the resulting forms in the learning, evaluation and communication environments used by the project. Testing will include accurate character and combination display, text entry and editing, and compatibility across the devices and software used during implementation. This is particularly important where the selected script involves complex shaping, combining marks or language-specific text behaviour. W3C language-enablement work similarly treats rendering, shaping, segmentation and line behaviour as part of effective script support on digital platforms.

Where a proposed orthography requires a character not currently encoded in Unicode, the programme will first determine whether the intended representation can be achieved using existing encoded characters or sequences. If genuinely new encoding is required, the technical work will document the requirement and assess the appropriate standards pathway. The project should not imply that formal Unicode encoding of a newly devised character can be guaranteed within the programme period.

The technical implementation will include collection and annotation infrastructure, learning and testing interfaces, candidate keyboards, font and rendering support, compatibility testing, deployment and technical documentation. The linguistic and research requirements will guide the technical implementation, while field and community conditions will inform practical usability. The programme will distinguish between shared infrastructure developed for the overall research workflow and candidate-specific digital resources, such as keyboards, font adaptations and encoding or compatibility solutions.

## Evidence Quality and Research Boundaries

Project work will be undertaken by trained community contributors, linguists, consultants and research assistants under appropriate scientific and technical supervision. Recording, transcription and linguistic analysis will follow defined protocols and quality standards. Project data, metadata, transcriptions, analyses and technical outputs will be systematically organised and maintained for review, validation and handover.

people.bio:
Dr. R. Karthick Narayanan is a linguist, digital archivist, and digital humanities specialist based in Chennai. He currently serves as the Executive Director and Co-founder of the Council for Diversity and Innovation (CoDIN) and as was previously the Chief Community and Data Officer at UnReal TecE LLP.

His work sits at the intersection of language, technology, and cultural preservation. He focuses on translational research and the infrastructure-documentation bridge, specifically applying AI and language technologies for social good. A core pillar of his work is the documentation and digital archiving of under-represented and indigenous languages in South Asia. Guided by the principles of epistemic justice and community-centered archiving—rooted in Respect, Relevance, Reciprocity, and Responsibility—he has been instrumental in public initiatives like the Tholkudi Digital Repository.

Beyond linguistics, his archival work extends into ethnomusicology, notably through the Suvadugal project, which involves the extensive documentation of traditional folk musical instruments and their acoustic identities.

As an accomplished scholar and writer, he co-authored the book Marum Ulagil Maraya Oligal (Sahitya Akademi), a work that earned him the SPARROW–R. Thyagarajan Literary Award.

people.name: Amalesh gope
people.bio:
Dr. Amalesh Gope is an Assistant Professor of Linguistics in the Department of Linguistics and Language Technology at Tezpur University, India. He completed his M.A. in Applied Linguistics at the University of Hyderabad and earned his PhD in Linguistics from the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Guwahati, with a thesis on the phonetics and phonology of Sylheti tonogenesis. His research interests include Acoustic Phonetics with special reference to Tone, Experimental and Prosodic Phonology, Computational Phonology and Intonation, Speech Technology and Digital Corpora, Image and Signal Processing (from ultrasound imaging to bio-colloids), Speech Perception, Language Documentation, and Machine Learning.
Dr. Gope has worked extensively on lesser-known and endangered languages of northeast India, including Sylheti, Noakhali, Goalparia, Bodo, Mog, Yimkhiung, Liangmai, Maram, Chokri, and others. He has delivered numerous invited talks and training workshops on speech and signal processing and computational linguistics at institutions across India, and has presented his research at international and national conferences in India and abroad.
He has published widely in internationally reputed journals, book chapters, and conference proceedings, and has edited six books. A co-authored monograph, Analyzing Linguistics Data Using Python and R, is forthcoming with Springer Nature. Dr. Gope has led and contributed to several externally funded research projects supported by MeitY (BHASHINI/National Language Translation Mission), DRDO, ICSSR, and DST, focused on building speech datasets, digital corpora, and language resources for under-resourced languages of the region.

content.teaser: Data Sovereignty, Data Quality and Indigenous Communities
content.markdown:
## The Goal

In today's AI-driven world, the digital divide is rapidly evolving into a profound social and economic divide. Despite our diverse real world, the digital landscape remains largely monolithic and non-inclusive. This lack of representation affects communities, languages, and cultures that don't fit the dominant technological paradigm.

Governments, civil society organisations, communities, and individuals are increasingly concerned about how sociocultural norms, languages, practices, and identities are represented in AI systems.
There's a pressing need for sensitive, unbiased representation that reflects our world's true diversity, not just the perspectives of dominant group.


## The Cost 

Despite numerous initiatives to create more inclusive AI systems, these efforts often fall short due to insufficient quality training data that properly represents diverse languages and cultures. Documentation shows that up to 35-40% of originally collected data must be discarded due to quality issues, even with robust methodologies and reputable organizations involved. This entails a huge cost in terms of time and resources involved in creating datasets. As a result, only few languages and communities could be supported in the technological world.


## The Gap

Currently, speech and language data collection is primarily handled by organisations, individuals and community members with little to no experience or training required for working with indigenous, underserved communities, resulting in fundamental misunderstandings of its unique requirements.

- **General annotation firms** lack specific training in working with diverse, indigenous communities.
- While skilled in community engagement, **civil society and community-based professionals** typically lack an understanding of linguistic complexity and linguistic field research expertise.
- **Language Promotion Organizations** are often focused on promoting specific language varieties rather than capturing linguistic diversity, thereby, filtering out, instead of collecting the required dataset.
- Even **academic departments** frequently lack proper fieldwork training and methodology for this specialized work.


## The W2M Intervention

The W2M Academy has designed this specialised course for training community members, researchers, civil society members and other stakeholders, who are engaged in or are planning to get engaged in data collection or AI model development. The course will train participants in the methods and practice of large-scale linguistic data collection and AI model development with indigenous communities. With our experts who have been working in linguistic field methods, language documentation and language technologies of indigenous and underserved communities for over a decade, this training and certification program aims to fill the community training and data quality gap.

activity.description: A government-supported cultural expression documentation and digital archiving initiative focused on preserving the traditional arts, performances, musical instruments, artist histories, and cultural knowledge systems of Tamil Nadu’s Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe communities. The project contributes to the safeguarding and long-term preservation of intangible cultural heritage in line with broader UNESCO cultural heritage preservation goals.

activity.title: Field Methods for Speech Technologies (Multilingual)
activity.description: A 6-day intensive residential course focusing on training community members, linguists and AI developers in data collection and model training pipelines for building ASR systems in Kurux and Sadri.

activity.title: Draft Curriculum Meeting on Arts-Based Personality Development Training for School and College Students
activity.description: The kick-off workshop for collaboration between CoDIN and Alternative Media Centre, a cooperative of artists in Tamil Nadu.

activity.title: Tholkudi
activity.description: A government-supported language and cultural documentation initiative focused on preserving the linguistic, oral, ecological, and cultural heritage of Tamil Nadu’s Scheduled Tribe communities through digital archiving, field documentation, and public access systems. The project contributes to safeguarding intangible cultural heritage through community-centered archival and documentation practices.

activity.title: Project Kailash
activity.description: Collecting large-scale training data across minoritised and tribal languages. Our mission is to reduce AI's bias by building fundamental benchmarking and training datasets for excluded cultures.
